GroupTrack — Quick Start

Getting you onto a trail with a map that works and a ride you can keep.

This is the short version. It covers the least you need to get going. Everything else — every panel, every option — is in the User Manual, which you can open any time from Help.

What GroupTrack is

An off-road trail app for side-by-side, UTV, ATV, dirt bike and Jeep riders. It holds the trails and the maps on your device, so it keeps working where there is no signal — which is most of where you ride.

First install

Grant the app the authorities it needs — all files, and GPS all the time. Follow the prompts.

Choose your home state and let it download the trails, so they work with no signal.

When the app loads your location, you are ready to play.

That is the whole of it. The detail below is worth reading when you have a moment — none of it is needed to get going.

Loading the trails for your home state

On first launch GroupTrack asks for file access and location, then asks which state you ride in and offers the one it thinks you are in.

[ SCREENSHOT: home state selection panel ]

Pick your state and let it run. It takes about twenty minutes and pulls a lot of data, so do it on wifi. It is not something to start at the trailhead.

What it is fetching, and why it takes that long: GroupTrack does not use one trail map. It pulls from every public source that covers your state and merges them, so a trail one agency published and another did not still appears. For Utah that is seven catalogues plus the OpenStreetMap extract:

  • Utah Trails and Pathways — the state's own trail record
  • US Forest Service, Bureau of Land Management, National Park Service, USGS National Trails — the federal agencies that manage the ground
  • Arizona State Parks — border coverage
  • OpenStreetMap — the largest single source, and the one that carries tracks and unclassified roads the agencies do not list

Another state draws on a different set. The app picks the sources that cover the area you asked for.

It also downloads the land ownership record for your state, which is what lets it tell public ground from private.

When it finishes you get a summary listing every source and what came in. It waits for you — if you put the tablet down and come back later, it is still there. ⚠ If a line says a source failed, the rest still loaded; you can reload the state later from the same place.
Choosing what appears on the map

GroupTrack holds around 146,000 trails for Utah. Most of what is in that number is ground you will never ride — footpaths, residential streets, cycle paths through town. Choosing what appears is how the map becomes readable.

[ SCREENSHOT: Map Features › Trails › SELECT ]

What you get out of the box

GroupTrack starts by showing motorized trails on public land only. Hiking, biking and equestrian trails are hidden, and so is private ground.

⚠ If a trail you know exists is not on the map, that is why — not a fault. It is a deliberate choice for an off-road app, and it is the first thing worth knowing.

Changing it

Map Features › Trails › SELECT. The same button you use to choose which tracks, waypoints or routes appear.

  • Include private land — one tick. Near a town this is what removes the residential street grid, which is usually why a map is hard to read there.
  • The trail types, in two columns: motorized and non-motorized. Tap a row to hide that type; tap a column heading for the whole group.

And OFF on the Trails row hides every trail in one tap, for when you want to see the ground.

The colours are yours

Solid lines are motorized. Dotted lines are not. That is the distinction worth learning, and it is one you can read in sunlight without picking colours apart.

Tap Map Keys to see what each line means, and tap any name in that list to change its colour, pattern or thickness. It shows the line as it is beside the line as it would be, so you can compare before committing. What you choose is saved.

How this goes

You do not have to take it all on at once. Most riders never go past the second step, and that is a complete and useful app.

1 · Ride and record
Trails on your device, maps that work with no signal, and a record of where you went. Nothing else required.
2 · Plan before you go
Build a route, or have the planner build several and compare them. Download the maps for it. Bring in what you already have from Gaia or onX.
3 · Ride as a group needs radios
See where everyone is, with no cell service. ⭐ A rider only needs a radio — no phone, no app. Someone hands them one and they appear on your map.

Each step is worth getting comfortable with before you reach for the next. The app does not mind which one you stop at.

Structure and navigation

GroupTrack is built from three surfaces. Everything the app does is reached from one of them, and the important thing to take away is use the right surface for the task.

1 · The Meshtastic radio surface optional
Everything to do with the radios. Turn it off if you ride with a phone or tablet alone — and turn it back on if you later move to group awareness.
2 · Your Ride Map
The map you use in the field, on the trail. Simple and focused — what you need while you are riding and nothing more.
3 · The Ride Planning Map
Built to be used online, at home. Design a route yourself or have the planner build one for you, download maps for offline use, and prepare for the ride. This is where the work happens before you go.

All navigation is text. Words you tap, down the right-hand side of either map. No icons to decode.

And the two maps carry the same controls in the same places — learn one and you know the other.

Down the right-hand side of either map is a short column of words. That is the whole of GroupTrack's navigation. Everything below is reached from one of them.

The Meshtastic navigation mesh only

Down the left-hand side is a second, separate navigation. That one belongs to Meshtastic, the radio software GroupTrack is built on — contacts, nodes, channels, connections.

If you have no radio, none of it is for you. The last item in that column is Hide Mesh — tap it and the whole column folds away.

When it is folded, a Mesh word appears in the right-hand column with the GroupTrack controls. Tap that to bring it back.

GroupTrack remembers which you chose.

I want to track my rides as an individual and will not use a mesh radio at this time.

You want trails, offline maps, and a record of where you went. Everything below is about that.

You will see radio panels you do not need. The list down the left side of the app belongs to Meshtastic, the radio software GroupTrack is built on. If you have no radio, none of it is for you. Ignore it.
Get comfortable — before you need it

Maps for where you are going

Trail lines are already on your device. The satellite and topo imagery underneath them is not. This is the one preparation that cannot be done at the trailhead.

Trail lines are one thing. The picture underneath them — satellite, topo — is another, and that comes from tile sources you choose.

There are three slots: SAT, TOPO and TOPO+. A list of public tile sources is offered, and any source can go in any slot.

[ SCREENSHOT: map sources selection ]

It works out of the box. The app ships already configured and you can ignore this entirely. But it is worth ten minutes, because the imagery under your trails is most of what you actually read on the trail.

Worth doing once

While you are at home and online, switch between the sources and look at your own area. They differ enormously — one will have current imagery where another is five years stale, and one will show a road the others do not. Settle on the three you prefer, then set them into SAT, TOPO and TOPO+.

For the SAT slot we recommend a satellite HYBRID — Google Hybrid, for instance. A plain satellite image is beautiful and tells you nothing about what anything is called. A hybrid carries the road and place labels over the imagery, which is what you want when you are working out where you are.

You do not need all three offline

When you download maps for an area you choose which sources come with it. Three sources means three times the download and three times the storage.

If you only want one offline, untick the others on the download. Those sources still work when you have a signal — you just will not have them on the trail.

⚠ Changing a source later replaces the imagery you have downloaded. The tiles on your device belong to the source they came from. Switch sources and you will need to refresh those areas to get the new imagery. Worth settling this before you download a lot.

Bringing in what you already have

If you use Gaia or onX, the tracks, trails and routes you have collected there come across as GPX files.

Export them from Gaia or onX. If you do that on this device the file lands in Downloads and GroupTrack will find it. If you exported somewhere else — another phone, a desktop — email it to yourself and save the attachment to Downloads.

⚠ There is no direct connection between the apps. It is export, then import, and the file passes through Downloads on the way.

Every GPX in Downloads is offered for import. Details of what happens to names, dates and duplicates are in the manual.

Building a route to follow

A route is a line you intend to ride, as opposed to a track, which is a record of one you did. Map Features › Route+ starts one, and there are two ways to build it.

  • Draw — you drop pins along the way. Where there are trails under you the route snaps to them; where there are none it draws straight between your points. The traditional method, and the one to use when you know exactly where you want to go.
  • AI Assisted — you give it a trailhead, how far you want to ride and any places you want to pass through, and it builds several routes for you out of the trail network. It then puts them side by side so you can compare distance, riding time and the trails each one uses.

Both are covered properly in the manual.

⭐ Go and press things. Every one of these is worth ten minutes at home with a cup of tea. Do not wait until you need something you have never used — a trailhead with no signal is a poor place to learn what a button does. Nothing here can break anything; the worst you can do is download a map you did not want.

Reading the map

1 · Know what you are looking at Solid lines are motorized. Dotted lines are not. That is the one thing worth learning before you set off. Colour separates the types within each group.
Tap Map Keys to see what each line means.
2 · Know what is hidden GroupTrack starts by showing motorized trails on public land only. Hiking and biking trails are hidden, and so is private ground.
If a trail you know exists is not there, that is why — not a fault. Change it under Map Features › Trails › SELECT.
3 · Download the maps for where you are going Trail lines are already on your device. The satellite and topo imagery underneath them is not. Use MAPS to download the area before you leave. Without it you get trails floating on a blank background.
4 · Have a look around Pan to where you ride and tap a trail. It opens a card showing everything known about it — surface, who manages it, any posted restrictions. Some trails carry a lot; many carry almost nothing.
More in the manual: planning a route the app builds for you, changing the trail colours, and what each trail type means.
Record your first ride — at home

⭐ Do this one around the block. Not on the trail — at home, where it does not matter. Press the button, drive to the shop and back, stop it, and look at what you got. Then you know exactly what happens before it counts.

1 · Start on the Ride Map That is the map you land on. Check you can see yourself and that the imagery around you has loaded.
2 · Press the red record button Press it before you set off, not once you are moving — the first part of a ride is usually the part you most want on the map afterwards.
3 · Put the device away and ride It keeps recording with the screen off. You do not need to keep it awake or keep the app in front.
4 · Press it again when you are done Your ride is saved to My tracks and drawn on the map in green. It stays on the device — nothing needs a signal.
Battery. Recording uses GPS the whole time. On a long day, bring a charger.
More in the manual: naming and tidying your tracks, sharing a ride, exporting to GPX, and turning a ride you liked into a route to follow again.
I want to use a Meshtastic radio with other riders in my group so we are all aware of all riders’ locations.

You want everything above plus the ability to see where the rest of your group is, with no cell service.

⭐ A rider only needs a radio. No phone, no tablet, no app. Someone hands them one and they appear on everyone else's map. A group of six needs one person running GroupTrack and five carrying radios — which is a much lower bar than getting everybody to install something.

⚠ One rider without a radio is invisible to the others. That is the only hard rule.

It works out of the box. Every install carries a GroupTrack default configuration that supports any group with no changes at all. The radio setup menu exists for one problem — two rides within a couple of miles of each other seeing each other's carts — and most riders will never open it.

Which radio

We recommend the T1000-e, and the reason is practical. It is the size of a credit card, the battery lasts about two days, and it wears on a lanyard — nothing to mount, wire, or remember to charge halfway through a trip.

⭐ It is also the one GroupTrack configures for you — about thirty seconds a radio, so a dozen is a few minutes at the trailhead.

⚠ Any other radio and you configure it yourself. The app gives you the settings; you apply them. If you have chosen a different radio you already know Meshtastic well enough to do that, and we will not pretend otherwise.

Clubs, and riders who know nothing about any of this

⭐ Because a rider needs only the radio, a club can buy a pool of them — about $45 each — hand them out at the trailhead and collect them afterwards.

The rider being handed one needs no knowledge, no app and no setup. They put it round their neck and they are on the map. That is the whole of their involvement.

A club configures its radios once and rides on its own network from then on. An ad-hoc group does not need to configure anything at all — the default works.

The radio

Pair it Turn the radio on and connect it over Bluetooth. The panels down the left side of the app are the radio's — pairing, channels and radio settings live there.
Get the group on one channel Radios only hear each other on a shared channel. Worth sorting out before the day rather than in the car park.
Make yourself identifiable Your radio carries a name. Set it to something the others will recognise — a group map of unnamed nodes helps nobody.
Test it with one other rider Stand apart, both radios on, and check you can see each other move. Ten minutes at home beats finding out at the trailhead.
The manual covers the radio properly — the full setup, channel settings, and what to check when a rider stops appearing.
Record your first ride — at home

⭐ Do this one around the block too, and if you can, with one other rider. Ten minutes at home tells you more than an hour of reading, and it is a far better place to discover a radio is not paired.

1 · Radio on and connected before you leave Check the app shows it connected. If it is not, you are recording a solo ride whether you meant to or not.
2 · Check you can see the others Before anyone sets off, confirm the group appears on the map. This is the moment to fix it, not three miles in.
3 · Press the red record button, then ride Your own ride records exactly as it does for any rider. The radio adds the others to your map; it does not change how your track is captured.
4 · Say who is leading If GroupTrack sees a group ride it asks you to pick the lead cart. That rider lays down a track the rest of the group follows on their maps — so the people behind can see the line the leader actually took, not just a dot moving about.
Where there are trails under the leader the track snaps to them. Where there are not, it draws straight between positions a few seconds apart, so a fast section across open ground looks straighter than it was ridden.
5 · Ride Positions update as people move. Range depends on terrain — a ridge between two riders will drop the link, and it comes back when it clears.
6 · Press it again when you are done Your ride is saved to My tracks, same as anyone's.
More in the manual: what the radio can and cannot do, expected range, and what to check when a rider stops appearing.
Download your maps, ride off grid, and know your way around the app before you hit the trails. Everything here is worth ten minutes at home with a cup of tea. A trailhead with no signal is a poor place to learn what a button does.

Something not working? Open Help and read the release notes for this version — a known problem is usually listed there. The full User Manual is in the same place, and it is your friend.
